transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Hurst.
Democratic Congresswoman Hailey Stevens is revoking her endorsement
of her former primary rival in the Michigan Senate race, Abdul El-Sayed.
And she says she's now backing his Republican opponent,
former Congressman Mike Rogers.
NPR's Sam Greenglass reports from Detroit.
Stevens has been criticizing El-Sayed for not doing enough
to win over many black and Jewish voters who backed her in the primary.
After trading seething statements in recent days,
a planned joint appearance at a church in Detroit fell apart.
El-Sayed spoke to reporters outside that event, which went on without her.
None of this matters. You know what matters?
There's a family. You can go like 15 minutes that way,
or 15 minutes that way, or 15 minutes that way.
And there are families who are preparing to send their kids to schools tomorrow
that look like they did 50 years ago.
They're worried about what they're going to feed their kids for lunch.
They're worried that if one of their kids gets sick,
they're not going to be able to pay the bills.
Those are the things that matter.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called Stevens' reversal a "despicable betrayal."
Holding the Michigan Senate seat is key for Democrats to retake the chamber.
Sam Greenglass, NPR News, Detroit.
States are reporting a surge of early voting
in a field that so far seems to be favoring Democrats.
NPR's Stephen Bassaha reports that the cost of living is at the top of many voters' minds.
Republicans were betting economic issues would be on their side
after they passed massive tax cuts last year.
This year, tax refunds have been about 12 percent larger than last.
But registered Republican Owen Smith in Des Moines, Iowa
says he can't remember if his tax refund was bigger.
I do my taxes like everyone else one time a year.
So any impact that that may have had on my thoughts at the time of voting
is way in the rear view compared to the gas prices that I'm seeing every single day.
Smith ended up splitting his ticket locally,
but voted for Democrats nationally due to the U.S. war against Iran.
Stephen Bassaha, NPR News.
And this with Election Day just two days away.
And Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy has been hospitalized following a stroke,
according to a statement from his office.
The Democrat is a popular campaign trail surrogate and possible 2028 presidential contender,
as NPR's Eric McDaniel reports.
Murphy's chief of staff, Alison Hewitt, released a statement.
It said the senator started experiencing numbness in his arm
while at his son's hockey game on Saturday
and was taken to a local hospital where it was discovered that he'd experienced a stroke.
The statement says Murphy was then transferred to Johns Hopkins Hospital for further monitoring
and was responding well to treatment and that doctors are encouraged by his progress.
Hewitt said Murphy is awake, alert, and expected to make a full recovery.
Murphy is known as a leader in the Democratic caucus,
particularly on his oversight of the Trump administration,
Eric McDaniel, NPR News Washington.
And you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
In Germany, rioters looted stores and clashed with police in Frankfurt yesterday,
injuring more than 100 officers, this following mostly peaceful demonstrations around the country
to lower the cost of living and improve education.
Thousands of people in dozens of cities took to the streets, including the capital, Berlin,
demanding more spending on schools, climate protection, and housing.
The protests coincided with Halloween,
and authorities blame infiltrators after it turned violent in some areas.
It mirrors similar protests that have rocked France over the past several weeks.
The town of Pagosa Springs, Colorado is bracing for extreme flooding tonight.
Local officials have issued mandatory evacuation orders.
From member station KSUT, Adam Burke has more.
Late last month, extreme flooding destroyed roads, buildings,
and critical infrastructure along several watersheds in southwest Colorado and northwest New Mexico.
This morning, the National Weather Service projected that the San Juan River
will rise to almost 20 feet in the town of Pagosa Springs.
Shattering historic records, the town and surrounding county have issued mandatory evacuation orders
for residents living in the area.
Counties along the Rio Grande River in southwest Colorado have issued pre-evacuation notices as well.
For NPR News, I'm Adam Burke in Durango.
At the weekend box office, the Elizabeth Holmes documentary, you can see everything.
Took the top spot again with an estimated $10 million in ticket sales in its third weekend.
In second place, Clay Face, a film about the Batman villain with $10 million.
I'm Janine Herfs, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Rep. Hailey Stevens revokes endorsement of Abdul El-Sayed and backs Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race
Early voting surges ahead of Election Day, with cost of living top of voters' minds, reports Stephen Bassaha
Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, his office says, expected to make full recovery
Riots in Frankfurt, Germany injure more than 100 police during cost-of-living and education protests
Pagosa Springs, Colorado orders mandatory evacuations as San Juan River flooding threatens record heights
Elizabeth Holmes documentary 'You Can See Everything' tops weekend box office for third straight weekend
